id: On the Existence of the Soul

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

How confident I am it is there. Don’t I bring it, As if it were enclosed in a fine leather case, To particular places solely for its own sake? Haven’t I set it down before the variegated canyon And the undeviating bald salt dome? Don’t I feed it on ivory calcium and ruffled Shell bellies, shore boulders, on the sight Of the petrel motionless over the sea, its splayed Feet hanging? Don’t I make sure it apprehends The invisibly fine spray more than once? I have seen that it takes in every detail I can manage concerning the garden wall and its borders. I have listed for it the comings and goings Of one hundred species of insects explicitly described. I have named the chartreuse stripe And the fimbriated antenna, the bulbed thorax And the multiple eye. I have sketched The brilliant wings of the trumpet vine and invented New vocabularies describing the interchanges between rocks And their crevices, between the holly lip And its concept of itself. And if not for its sake, why would I go Out into the night alone and stare deliberately Straight up into 15 billion years ago and more? I have cherished it. I have named it. By my own solicitations I have proof of its presence.

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of the text, refined for greater eloquence and flow while preserving all of its original meaning:

How certain I am of its presence. Do I not carry it,
As though it were sheathed in fine leather,
To particular places solely for its own sake?
Have I not set it down before the many-hued canyon
And the unwavering, barren salt dome?
Do I not nourish it on ivory calcium and the ruffled
Bellies of shells, on shore boulders, on the sight
Of the petrel poised motionless above the sea, its splayed
Feet dangling? Do I not ensure it perceives
The invisibly fine spray more than once?

I have watched it absorb every detail
I could offer of the garden wall and its borders.
I have catalogued for it the comings and goings
Of one hundred species of insects, each explicitly described.
I have named the chartreuse stripe
And the fringed antenna, the bulbous thorax
And the compound eye. I have sketched
The brilliant blossoms of the trumpet vine and devised
New vocabularies to describe the exchanges between rocks
And their crevices, between the holly's lip
And its conception of itself.

And were it not for its sake, why would I venture
Out into the night alone and gaze deliberately
Straight upward into fifteen billion years ago and beyond?

I have cherished it. I have named it.
Through my own devotions,
I hold proof of its presence.

Would you like me to offer an alternative version that stays even closer to the original phrasing, or one that leans further toward formal refinement?
outputs.L2:
How certain I feel that it exists. Don't I carry it, as though it were tucked inside a beautiful leather pouch, to specific locations for no reason but itself? Haven't I positioned it in front of the many-colored canyon and the perfectly smooth, bare salt dome? Don't I nourish it with white calcium and rippling shell undersides, coastal rocks, and with the view of the storm bird suspended above the ocean, its spread feet dangling? Don't I ensure that it perceives, on more than one occasion, the impossibly delicate mist?

I have watched it absorb every particular I can offer about the garden wall and its edges. I have catalogued for it the arrivals and departures of a hundred kinds of insects, each one clearly detailed. I have identified the yellow-green stripe and the fringed feeler, the swollen thorax and the compound eye. I have drawn the dazzling wings of the trumpet vine and created fresh languages to capture the exchanges between stones and their cracks, between the holly's edge and its notion of what it is.

And if not for its benefit, why else would I venture alone into the darkness and gaze intentionally upward, directly into fifteen billion years past and beyond? I have treasured it. I have given it a name. Through my own earnest appeals, I possess evidence that it is here.
outputs.L3:
# The Precious Unnamed

I carry something precious with me always, though I cannot give it a name. I treat it with the tenderness one reserves for the most fragile of treasures, as if it were cradled within a fine leather case, protected from every jolt and scratch the world might offer. It travels with me everywhere, a presence I guard and cherish beyond all reckoning.

Deliberately, I expose this presence to the wild variety of the earth. I bring it before the great canyons that split the land open to reveal their layered depths, and to the strange swelling of salt domes rising from the ground. I carry it to the edges of seashores where the water meets the sand, and I hold it still beneath the petrels that hover on the wind above the waves. I want it to know the vividness of these places, their color and their strangeness.

With great care, I feed it the smallest sensory details of the living world. I offer it the intricate architecture of insects, the delicate structures of plants, the rough and patient surfaces of rocks. I catalog each feature meticulously, and when the old words fail me, I invent new vocabularies—fresh language capable of holding what I have witnessed, so that nothing might be lost or left undescribed.

And when the day is done, I venture alone into the darkness. There, beneath the open sky, I let this presence gaze upward into the vast depths of cosmic time, into the light of stars that have traveled across billions of years to reach us. I let it contemplate the enormity of it all, the near-eternity written across the heavens.

Through all of this—through the cherishing, the naming, the patient and attentive solicitation—I claim that I have found my proof. In the very act of loving something so completely, of tending to it and calling it into being through my care, I have discovered the evidence of its existence.
outputs.L4:
# On Perception as Proof: A Reading

The poem unfolds as an extended act of attention, cataloging the natural world in all its startling particularity. We move from salt domes rising through geological strata to petrels skimming the waves, from the intricate segmented architecture of insect anatomy to the light of stars that has traveled billions of years to reach us. These images do not arrive at random. Each is offered with care, laid down like an offering, as though the sheer specificity of the world could be marshaled toward a purpose larger than description.

That purpose is the poem's quiet engine. The speaker is devoted to something—an unnamed "it" that hovers behind every image without ever being pinned down. We sense it is the soul, or consciousness, or whatever we might call the tender, invisible core that makes us more than matter. The speaker does not argue for its existence through logic or doctrine. Instead, the effort is one of nourishment: to feed this intangible thing, to name the world so thoroughly and lovingly that the naming itself becomes a kind of sustenance. To attend to the salt dome, the petrel, the ancient starlight is to keep something alive.

What emerges, then, is a profound claim about the relationship between perception and being. The accumulated evidence of care—the long, patient catalog of things noticed and cherished—becomes what the poem calls its "proof of presence." The soul cannot be measured or displayed, but it can be demonstrated indirectly, through the quality of a person's attention to the world. If the speaker can look this closely, love this deliberately, and hold the world's details this tenderly, then surely the thing doing the looking must exist.

In this way, the poem suggests that consciousness confirms itself through the act of cherishing. We do not first possess a soul and then use it to perceive; rather, the disciplined labor of perception is what affirms and sustains the essence being sought. To notice is to nourish. To name is to confirm. The intangible "it" is not found at the end of the search but enacted continuously in the searching itself—kept present, moment by moment, through the devoted work of paying attention.
outputs.L5:
# Finding Haven

How does a person know when they've finally found the place they belong? For Don, the answer arrived quietly, without fanfare, on an ordinary autumn afternoon.

Don had spent most of his life searching. He moved from city to city, chasing jobs, chasing opportunities, and sometimes chasing nothing more than the vague hope that the next place would feel like home. Yet no matter where he landed, a restless emptiness followed him. He often asked himself *how* he might ever settle down when contentment seemed to slip through his fingers.

The turning point came when a friend invited him to visit a small coastal town called Haven. The name struck Don as almost too fitting, and he nearly laughed at the irony. Still, he packed a bag and made the drive, expecting little more than a pleasant weekend.

But Haven surprised him. It was not the scenery alone—though the harbor glowed golden at sunset—nor the slow, unhurried rhythm of the streets. It was the way strangers greeted him warmly, the way time seemed to expand rather than rush past. For the first time in years, Don felt his shoulders relax.

As the days passed, he began to understand *how* belonging works. It isn't about finding a perfect place; it's about finding a place that welcomes your imperfections. Haven did exactly that. Don stopped running, rented a small cottage near the water, and slowly built a life he no longer wanted to escape.

Looking back, Don realized the question was never really *how* to find happiness. The real question was whether he was brave enough to stop searching and simply stay. In Haven, at last, he was.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in which the speaker never directly names what "it" is, but proves its existence through acts of attention, observation, and cataloging the natural world.
counterfactuals.output:
# Evidence

I have never seen it, but I know
the way a botanist knows the unnamed flower
by its habit of turning east,
by the particular geometry of its leaving.

Consider: the sparrow does not doubt.
It builds against a coming cold
it cannot yet feel, threading dry grass
through the crook of a branch as if instructed.

I have counted the rings inside the fallen oak—
two hundred summers written in a wrist of wood,
each drought a tightness, each good year
a generous widening—and someone kept that ledger.

Watch how the tide returns.
Watch how the salmon climbs its own long argument
upstream, against all reasonable water,
toward the exact gravel where it started.

I am only cataloging.
The moth that finds the moon inside a streetlamp.
The way frost ferns across the glass
in patterns no hand drew, and yet were drawn.

Call it what you will, or do not call it.
I offer no proof but the proof of looking:
the mushroom pushing its slow lantern up through leaves,
the mantis folded in its green devotion.

Something insists.
I have seen it insist in the pale root
splitting the sidewalk, in the way
even the ruined field remembers how to green.

I will not say the word.
But I have knelt in the wet grass at dawn
and found the whole meadow strung with evidence—
a thousand webs, each holding its bright, deliberate rain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem in the style of Pattiann Rogers, using rhetorical questions and vivid natural imagery to suggest the presence of the soul or spirit.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Body Knows of Wind

Consider the way a heron holds
itself at the water's edge—one leg
folded like a question into feathers,
the yellow eye unblinking. Is this
patience, or is it something older,
some knowing that precedes the fish,
precedes the hunger, precedes even
the long blue architecture of the wing?

And when the cottonwood releases
its seed to the June air, ten thousand
small white parachutes drifting
above the creek, who taught the tree
this generosity, this letting go?
Is there a spirit in the loosening,
a soul in the surrender, some invisible
hand that opens the closed fist of the pod?

I want to know what moves inside
the salamander wintering under stone,
its slow heart barely troubling the dark.
What dreams the bear, curled in the earth's
own body, breathing once a minute
into the black? Is there a light
that does not require the eye to see it,
a music the ear was never made to hold?

Perhaps the soul is what the field mouse
carries in its quick blood, what flares
in the firefly's brief and yellow lantern,
what the whale sings across four hundred
miles of ocean dark. Perhaps it is
the reaching—the vine toward the trellis,
the root toward water, the sunflower
turning its enormous face all day
to follow what it cannot name but needs.

And here, at dusk, when the swallows
stitch the air above the barn
and the first star pierces the failing light—
tell me, is this not evidence enough?
This wanting to praise, this ache
to gather the whole world into words,
this hunger in me that leans, that leans,
that leans toward something I have never
seen but somehow, in my marrow, know.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemplative poem where the speaker treats an unnamed inner presence like a companion they carry to beautiful places—canyons, seashores, gardens—to let it perceive the world.
counterfactuals.output:
# What I Carry

I brought you to the canyon's edge today,
where light falls red through millions of years of stone,
and stood a while so you could feel the way
the wind moves through a place that's mostly bone.

You have no eyes, and yet I hold you up
the way one lifts a child to see parade—
here is the sea, its silver, breaking cup,
here is the shade the cypresses have made.

I do not know your name. I never have.
You were the quiet listener all along,
the one who stayed when other things would leave,
the small persistent hunger to belong.

So I have made myself your open door.
The garden now: the roses heavy, low,
the bees at work, the warm and drowsy floor
of afternoon. I brought you here to know

that beauty was not something I withheld,
that even in the years I walked alone
I meant to show you everything I beheld—
to carry you toward all I could have shown.

And when at last I set you gently down,
or when the carrier and the carried blur,
let it be here, where evening stains the ground
and something in me finally learns to *see*—

not for myself, but for the one I bore
through canyons, gardens, down along the shore.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem about how the act of naming, describing, and paying close attention to nature becomes evidence for something intangible we carry within us.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Naming Knows**

Before I learned the word *sycamore*,
the tree was only shade and shifting light—
now every peeling patch of bark
is a syllable I've come to love,
a proof of some attention
I did not know I owned.

To call the heron *heron*
is to admit I stopped,
that something in me leaned
toward the still gray patience at the water's edge
and would not let it pass unmarked.

We do not name what we ignore.
The words are footprints, evidence
that we were here, that we were moved,
that the mind reached out
and touched the ordinary miracle
of goldenrod, of wren, of frost
etching its brief geometry
across the windowpane.

Each careful noticing—
the way the light comes sideways in October,
the particular hush before the rain—
is testimony to a self
that cannot be dissected or displayed,
that lives in the *between*:
between the eye and the leaf,
between the breath and the naming of the breath.

So let me keep this ledger of the world,
this catalog of small devotions,
not to possess what I describe
but to leave a record
of the invisible thing that looked,
that lingered,
that found the field worth learning by heart—

and in the learning, learned itself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem full of rhetorical questions ("Don't I...", "Haven't I...") in which a speaker offers detailed natural observations—insects, petrels, tidal spray, the night sky—as proof of the soul's existence.
counterfactuals.output:
**Testimony**

Haven't I watched the mayfly spend its one
gold afternoon above the reddening pond,
its wings a thread of isinglass and sun,
and felt some answering thinness in my chest?
Don't I contain what quivers past the bond
of one day's flight, some flame that will not rest?

Haven't I seen the petrels walk the swell,
their black feet stitching hem to running hem,
the way they read the water like a spell
no compass writes, no charted current shows?
And if the sea speaks secretly to them,
don't I hear something too, that no one knows?

Haven't I stood where tidal spray came up
in slow white detonations on the rocks,
each drop a lens, a momentary cup
that held the whole gray morning and let go?
If matter learns to mirror and unlocks,
don't I hold light the way that spindrift does—

and give it back? Haven't I lain awake
beneath the wheeling, cold, indifferent stars,
the Pleiades a smudge of frozen ache,
Orion strung across the roof of black,
and felt the distance close, as if the far
long-traveled light had come to call me back?

Don't I? For nothing dead attends so well.
No stone leans toward the moth, no clod is stirred
by wingbeat, foam, or that far bright farewell
the night sky offers nightly to the eye.
But I lean out. I listen. I have heard.
And what leans out to listen cannot die.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
